planting.note: Set out container-grown offsets or rooted pups in spring once nights stay reliably above 50°F; this slow-growing giant bromeliad takes years to bulk up into a landscape-scale rosette and is hardy in the ground only in zone 9b-11.

directions: Grow in fast-draining, coarse soil or a bark-based mix in bright filtered light to part sun; some direct sun deepens the foliage color toward bronze-purple, while hotter, unshaded exposures in the Deep South can scorch the broad leaves. Alcantarea imperialis is a massive terrestrial bromeliad native to rocky cliffs and coastal mountains in southeastern Brazil, forming an enormous, flattened rosette of thick, leathery, strap-shaped leaves that can take a decade to reach full size before it blooms. Once mature, a single rosette sends up a tall, stout, candelabra-like flower stalk bearing clusters of pale flowers well above the foliage, after which that rosette dies back while offsets around its base continue the clump. Keep the central cup topped off with water where practical, let the coarse growing medium dry between waterings, and protect plants from temperatures below the upper 20s°F, since this species has no frost tolerance and is grown in large containers for overwintering north of zone 9b.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery-grown offsets in spring once nights stay above 50°F; this wine-red color form of the imperial bromeliad is slow to reach landscape size and is reliably hardy outdoors only in zone 9b-11.

directions: Site in bright, filtered light to part sun in fast-draining, coarse soil; brighter light intensifies the deep wine-red to maroon leaf color that distinguishes this selection from the plain green species, while heavier shade keeps the rosette greener and looser. This named color form of Alcantarea imperialis forms the same massive, flattened landscape-scale rosette as the species but with rich burgundy foliage that holds its tone through the seasons, making it a sought-after focal point in South Florida and Gulf Coast tropical gardens. After many years a mature rosette produces a tall, stout flowering stalk above the leaves, and that rosette then declines while pups forming around its base carry the clump forward. Keep the central cup filled with water where practical, water sparingly at the roots between dry spells, and bring container specimens under cover or into a protected microclimate whenever temperatures threaten to drop into the 20s°F, since this form shares the species' lack of frost tolerance.

planting.note: Set out container-grown offsets in spring once nights stay above 50°F; this large Brazilian bromeliad is grown in-ground in zone 9b-11 and in containers with winter protection elsewhere.

directions: Grow in coarse, fast-draining soil in bright filtered light to part sun, which keeps the broad, silvery, cross-banded leaves from scorching while still supporting good color and eventual flowering. Alcantarea odorata is a large terrestrial bromeliad from Brazil's rocky coastal escarpments, forming a wide, symmetrical rosette of stiff, arching leaves that becomes dusted with a silvery-white farina as it matures. Once the rosette is fully grown, it sends up a tall branched flower spike bearing pale, noticeably scented flowers that give the species its name — a trait that sets it apart from most other giant bromeliads, which are showy but unscented. Keep the central cup filled with water where practical, let the growing medium dry between waterings, and shelter plants from temperatures below the upper 20s°F, since this species is killed by hard frost and relies on container culture for overwintering outside zone 9b-11.

planting.note: Set out rooted offsets or container-grown plants in spring once nights stay above 50°F; this heat- and drought-tolerant landscape bromeliad is grown in-ground in zone 9b-11 and in large containers farther north.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in part sun to light shade; stronger light intensifies the reddish flush of the leaves while a bit of afternoon shade is useful protection during the hottest Gulf Coast summers. Androlepis skinneri is a large, clump-forming terrestrial bromeliad from Central America and southern Mexico with stiff, broad, spine-edged leaves radiating out in a bold rosette, long used as a tough architectural accent in South Florida landscaping since it was first introduced from wild Nicaraguan stock. A mature rosette produces a thick, upright flower stalk topped with clustered, snow-white blooms well above the foliage, after which pups forming around the base keep the planting going for years. It tolerates considerable heat and drought once established and needs little irrigation beyond occasional watering of the central cup and surrounding soil, but foliage is damaged below the upper 20s°F and the plant is killed by a hard freeze, so it is grown as a container specimen with winter protection outside zone 9b-11.
